title: Two kinds of inability (1): lack of something the will cannot supply
source_text: XVIII. Caeterum Doctor ille, & qui cum eo sentiunt, pertendunt eam bene agendi impotentiam, quae reperitur in omnibus illis, qui destituti sunt gratia Christi ad haec vel illa bona opera necessaria, non tollere obligationem qua tenentur illa facere, nec eos excusare, quominus hac in parte officio suo fungantur. Atque ut hoc ostendant, notant duplicem esse praecepti faciendi impotentiam. Una est, inquiunt, ex defectu alicujus, quod non potest quantumlibet magna voluntate, hoc est quantumlibet fortiter volendo, suppleri. Talis est impotentia illius qui caret rebus temporalibus ad largiendam eleemosynam, & scientia ad eum docendum qui defectu instructionis perit, & hujusmodi infinita. De tali impotentia verissimum est, quod Deus non jubet impossibilia. Nam hoc ipso quo talis oritur impossibilitas, vel praeceptum extinguitur, vel certe ad illud implendum, is cui praecipitur, non amplius obligatus est. In hujusmodi etiam impossibilibus voluntas pro facto reputatur. Non est enim culpa voluntatis quod non fiat, sed pura inopia potestatis.
pass_a_gloss: XVIII. However that Doctor, and those who think with him, maintain that that inability of acting well, which is found in all those, who are destitute of the grace of Christ necessary for these or those good works, does not take away the obligation by which they are bound to do them, nor excuse them, from performing their duty in this part. And that they may show this, they note that the inability of doing a precept is twofold. One is, they say, from the defect of something, which cannot be supplied by however great a will, that is by willing however strongly. Such is the inability of him who lacks temporal goods for giving alms, and knowledge for teaching him who perishes through defect of instruction, and infinite things of this kind. Of such inability it is most true, that God does not command impossible things. For by the very fact that such impossibility arises, either the precept is extinguished, or certainly to fulfil it, he to whom it is commanded, is no longer obligated. In impossibles of this kind also the will is reputed for the deed. For it is not the fault of the will that it is not done, but pure want of power.
pass_b_english: Thesis XVIII. That doctor and those who share his view insist, however, that the inability to do good found in everyone who lacks the grace of Christ needed for this or that good work does not cancel their obligation to do it, nor excuse them from doing their duty in that respect. To prove it they point out that there are two kinds of inability to carry out a commandment.

'One kind,' they say, 'comes from the lack of something that no amount of will, that is, no strength of willing, can make up. Such is the inability of someone who has no worldly goods to give alms, or no knowledge to teach a person perishing for want of instruction, and countless cases like these. Of this inability it is perfectly true that God does not command the impossible. The moment such an impossibility arises, either the commandment lapses or at least the person commanded is no longer bound to fulfil it. In impossibilities of this kind the will is also counted as the deed, since the failure to act is not the will's fault but sheer lack of power.'

lemmas.gloss: does not take away the obligation
God does not command impossible things
the will is reputed for the deed

choices.why: Jansenius's impotentia: a lack of power to do something, not 'impotence'.

bible_refs: Cornelius Jansenius, Augustinus (Louvain, 1640), tome 3, De gratia Christi Salvatoris.
Augustine, De natura et gratia 43.50 ('Deus impossibilia non jubet'), taken up by the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 11.
